transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you. Well, honestly, I'm just... I'm really struggling at work right now, and it's getting to the point where I'm terrified I'm going to get fired. I work at a meat processing plant—mostly on the floor handling the cuts, but there's a ton of compliance and safety stuff you have to do at the end of the shift. I actually just finished my bachelor's degree, which was a whole other ordeal just to get through, but I took this job because it pays decent and I really needed something steady, you know? 

But the thing is, the plant has these incredibly strict protocols. Which makes sense, obviously, it's food safety, you can't mess around with that. But what brings me in is that... well, I keep starting things like the sanitation steps, the batch logs, or the end-of-line paperwork, and then I just... I somehow completely leave out the last parts of them. 

And it's not like I don't know how important it is! I *know* my job depends on finishing every single step correctly. I'll be doing the batch log, filling out the times and the weights and everything, and I'll get through like 80 percent of it, and then I'll just... put the clipboard down to check a temperature gauge or grab a sanitizer hose, and my brain just entirely drops the fact that the paperwork wasn't finished. Or I'll be doing the chemical wash for the cutting stations, and I'll do step one and two perfectly, and then somehow step three just completely evaporates from my mind. 

My supervisor pulled me aside on Tuesday—or was it Wednesday? No, Tuesday, because it was right after the big delivery truck came in—and he was just looking at me like I was doing it on purpose, holding this half-finished log. And I just stood there feeling so stupid because I *know* how to do it, I *want* to do it right, but I just keep leaving the ends off of everything I start. It's like my brain just checks out right before the finish line, every single time, and no matter how hard I try to force myself to just finish the form or finish the cleaning cycle, I still walk away before it's actually done.
Are you experiencing difficulties completing tasks or forgetting things outside of your job as well?

Honestly, I haven't really noticed it happening outside of work. Like, I mean, I guess I'm pretty focused on work right now because it's just so stressful, you know? The stakes are just so high there with the food safety and my supervisor breathing down my neck. So when I'm home, I don't know, I just kind of crash. I live in this little apartment, and it's pretty low-maintenance, so there aren't these huge, multi-step protocols I have to follow just to make dinner or do my laundry. I mean, sure, sometimes laundry sits in the basket for a few days, but that's just normal, right? Everyone does that. It's not like the batch logs where if I don't sign off on the exact chemical concentration at exactly 4:00 PM, the whole line gets shut down and I get written up. 

So, yeah, I don't think I'm having those same kinds of... catastrophic drop-offs at home. Or if I am, they just don't matter as much, so they don't register. Like, if I forget to finish a cup of coffee and leave it on the counter, nobody is going to fire me over it. But at the plant, every single little thing is tracked, and that's where I'm just completely falling apart. It's the paperwork, the sanitation steps, the specific sequence of things... that's where my brain just hits a wall. So, no, I wouldn't say it's an issue outside of the plant. At least, not that I'm aware of.
Do you feel anxious in other situations beyond your job at the meat processing plant?

No, not really. I mean, I don't think so. It's really just the job. Like, if I'm just hanging out at home or going to the grocery store or whatever, I feel completely fine. Normal, I guess. I don't get that tight feeling in my chest or that panic where my heart starts racing like it does when I'm looking at a half-finished sanitation log and realizing I missed a step again. 

Honestly, before I started at the plant, I wouldn't have called myself an anxious person at all. Even during college—and college was hard, don't get me wrong, I had to pull a lot of all-nighters to get my papers done because I'd always leave them to the absolute last minute, which was stressful, but it wasn't this constant, overwhelming dread. It was just typical student stress, you know? 

But now, it's like the second I pull into the parking lot at work, my stomach just drops. I look at the big metal doors and I just know, I *know* I'm going to mess something up that day. And it's just so specific to the plant because of how rigid everything is. Like, if I'm hanging out with my friends on the weekend—which I haven't been doing as much lately because I'm just so exhausted from being stressed at work all week—but when I do, I'm totally relaxed. We'll just be sitting on the couch watching a movie or getting food, and I don't feel anxious at all. I'm not worrying about whether I left a door unlocked or if I forgot to turn the oven off or anything like that. 

It really is just this intense, paralyzing fear of getting fired because I can't seem to just finish a simple checklist at work. It's like my anxiety is entirely tied to that one specific building and those specific clipboards. So outside of that? No, I wouldn't say I'm an anxious person. Just... really, really scared of losing this job.
Do you have difficulty paying attention to details in general?

Well, I mean, I don't think it's a general thing. Like, if you mean do I just not notice things in everyday life, no, I don't think so. I mean, I guess it really depends on what you mean by details, because there are some things I notice perfectly fine, you know? Like if I'm watching a movie, I can pick up on little plot clues, or if I'm talking to a friend, I can tell if they're upset even if they don't say anything. So it's not like I walk around completely oblivious to the world.

But... well, I guess if you're talking about the kind of details they care about at the plant, then... I mean, I guess I do struggle with those, but again, I really feel like that's just because it's the plant. It's not like a general flaw in my personality or something. It's just that the details at work are so incredibly specific and boring and repetitive. Like, checking the exact temperature of the wash water—it has to be exactly between 140 and 145 degrees, and you have to write it down on this tiny little line on the form, and you have to do it every single hour. And honestly, it's just so hard to care about that specific detail when you've already done it four times that shift and it's always the same. 

So, I guess sometimes I might gloss over those kinds of details, but I really don't think it's a problem I have in general. Like, I don't go to the grocery store and buy the wrong brand of cereal because I wasn't paying attention to the label, or accidentally put salt in my coffee instead of sugar. It's really just those tedious, repetitive work things where my brain just kind of slides right off the details. So, no, in general, I think I'm fine with details. It's just... the clipboard stuff.
Do you ever feel mentally foggy or confused at work?

Well, foggy... I mean, I guess you could call it that, but it's more like my brain just kind of... disconnects? Like, I'll go into a shift, right? And I'll be in the locker room putting on my hairnet and my boots, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, today is the day. Today I am going to stay completely focused, I'm going to check every single box, I'm going to do everything perfectly." And I really mean it! I start off trying so, so hard to stay completely locked in on what I'm doing. 

But then... I don't know, it's like the environment just wears me down. The noise of the machinery is always humming, and it's cold, and the line is moving, and you're just doing the same thing over and over. And after a while, all the cutting, the weighing of the portions, checking the expiration dates on the labels... it all just starts to blur together into this one big, monotonous smear of activity. 

And then, suddenly, I'll kind of snap back to reality and realize I've just been standing there, staring at the same tray of meat or the same line on the log sheet for who knows how long, completely blanking on what I'm actually supposed to be doing next. It's like the information is right there in front of my eyes, but it's just not registering in my brain anymore. I'm looking at the clipboard, and I know it's English, I know what the words mean, but I can't for the life of me figure out what the next step is. It's not that I'm confused about how to do my job—I know the protocols, I really do—it's just that my brain refuses to hold onto the thread of what I'm doing for more than a couple of hours. It just drifts off into this weird, blank space, and then I have to panic-scramble to figure out where I left off before the supervisor notices I've been staring at a wall. So, yeah, I guess foggy is a good word for it, but it's really just this complete inability to keep my brain engaged, no matter how hard I try to force it at the start of the shift.
Do you have physical symptoms like a racing heart or sweating when you're at work and worried about making mistakes?

Well, I mean, like I was saying earlier about the sanitation logs, I definitely get the racing heart. That's for sure. It feels like it's just going to pound right out of my chest when I realize I've skipped a step or forgotten to record a temperature check. 

But as for sweating... I don't really think so? Or, well, I guess I haven't really noticed if I do. You have to remember, the plant is kept freezing cold. It's a meat processing facility, so everything has to be strictly temperature-controlled to prevent bacteria, so it's always, like, thirty-four degrees or something out on the floor. Because of that, I have to wear all these layers just to survive a shift. I've got my regular clothes, and then thermal underwear, and then the heavy company-issued smock over that, plus the thick insulated rubber boots and the hairnet and the hard hat and the cut-resistant gloves. So honestly, even if I was sweating from the stress of it all, I probably wouldn't even be able to tell through all those layers of clothing. 

But I don't get that classic, you know, wiping-sweat-off-my-forehead kind of thing. It's more just... this horrible, internal dropping sensation. Like when you miss a step going down the stairs, but it lasts for ten minutes. My chest gets super tight, and my heart just goes crazy, and I just kind of freeze up holding my clipboard, terrified that my supervisor is going to walk around the corner. He's this guy named Dave, and he's always looking over everyone's shoulders, so the second I realize my brain just completely blanked out on the last three batches and I have no idea what the weights were, it's just pure, internal panic. But yeah, no, not sweating, as far as I know. Just the heart pounding and that awful tight feeling.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with friends or family since you started experiencing these difficulties at work?

Changes in my relationships? Um... I don't think so. I mean, not really. I guess it kind of depends on what you mean by changes, but honestly, I don't think my work stuff is really spilling over into my personal life like that. 

Like, I just got my degree recently, right? So a lot of my friends from college are either still finishing up their own programs or they've moved away to different cities for these fancy entry-level office jobs, so we mostly just text or FaceTime anyway. And when we do talk, I don't really bring up the whole clipboard thing or the fact that my brain keeps totally blanking out on the line. It's just... it's really hard to explain to someone who isn't standing in a thirty-four-degree room covered in heavy gear, smelling like raw poultry, you know? They're all talking about their emails or grad school applications, and I just feel like I can't really be like, "Yeah, I stared at a sanitation log for twenty minutes today and almost had a heart attack because I forgot to write down a number." So I just kind of keep all that to myself. We still talk about the same stuff we always did. 

And as for my family, I'm living at home with my parents right now to save up some money, and they know the job is hard, but we don't fight about it or anything. Honestly, by the time I get home from a shift, I am just so physically and mentally drained from trying to force my brain to pay attention for eight hours straight that I don't even have the energy to interact with anyone anyway. I basically just walk in the door, peel off all my thermal layers, and take a really, really long, hot shower to get the smell of the plant off me—because it really lingers, it's this weird, metallic, raw meat smell that gets right into your pores—and then I just crash in my room and scroll on my phone until I fall asleep. 

So, I mean, if anything, maybe I'm a little quieter at home just because I'm so exhausted? But no, there hasn't been any big drama or people getting mad at me, or me ruining friendships over it. The problems I'm having with focusing and everything, that really just stays at the plant. So, no, no real changes with my friends or family. Just me being really tired.
Do you think you're avoiding certain tasks at work or do you feel like you're genuinely unable to complete them?

Avoiding or unable... wow, um, that's a really interesting way to put it. Because, well, with the actual line work and the logs, it really does feel like I'm just genuinely unable to do it once my brain shuts off, like I was saying. But... if I'm being completely honest, there are definitely other parts of the job where I know I am absolutely, one hundred percent avoiding things. Like, actively running away from them. 

For example, because it's a meat processing facility, there is a ton of red tape. We have all these strict USDA guidelines, and OSHA safety standards, and cross-contamination rules, which I completely understand because, obviously, food safety is incredibly important. But because of all that, we have to do these periodic certification modules. And they give us these huge, dense packets of updated procedure reading that we're supposed to go through. 

And I just... I can't. I mean, I put off the certification modules and any of that really long procedure reading until the absolute last possible minute. Every single time. It's actually kind of ridiculous because I'll find literally anything else to do just to avoid it. I will volunteer to go back into the freezing cold room and scrub down the stainless steel prep tables again, or reorganize the heavy boxes of packaging materials, just so I don't have to go sit in the breakroom and look at those documents. 

It's just that sitting there, staring at a computer screen or a stack of papers, trying to actually absorb all those rules and regulations... it feels almost physically exhausting. Like, my brain just completely rejects it. Trying to force myself to read through paragraph after paragraph about proper temperature gradients or whatever, it feels like I'm trying to wade through waist-deep mud. It drains every single ounce of energy I have, way more than standing on my feet for eight hours does. 

So I just keep pushing it off and pushing it off until my supervisor, Dave—the guy I mentioned earlier—is literally standing there telling me that I can't clock in for my next shift unless I finish the online module. And then I have to sit there in a total panic, clicking through it as fast as I can, just completely exhausted by the effort of trying to make the words make sense. So, yeah, I guess with the reading and the modules, it's definitely avoidance. But it's avoidance because the mental effort required to do it just feels entirely impossible to summon.
Do you feel like you're not trying hard enough to complete your tasks at work, or do you feel like you're trying your best but still can't seem to finish them?

Oh, I am definitely trying my best. I mean, honestly, it almost hurts how hard I'm trying. That’s the most frustrating part of all of this, I think, and it's why I feel so defeated by the end of the day. Because I’ll walk into the plant at the beginning of my shift, right? I've got all my thermal layers on, my smock, my hard hat, I've had my coffee, and I literally tell myself in the locker room, "Okay, today you are going to focus. You are going to pay attention to every single detail and not mess up." 

And I really, genuinely start the shift trying so incredibly hard to stay locked in. I'm double-checking my clipboard, I'm watching the line, I'm making sure I'm doing everything perfectly. But then... I don't know, it's like my brain just runs out of battery or something. Because after a while, all the different tasks—the cutting the meat, the weighing of the batches, checking the expiration labels on the packaging—it all just completely blurs together into this endless, monotonous loop. The noise of the machinery and the cold just kind of wash over me, and before I even realize it's happening, my brain just checks out. 

I’ll suddenly snap back to reality and realize that I’ve been standing there staring at the exact same tray of poultry, or just staring at the exact same line on my log sheet for who knows how long, just completely blank. I'm looking right at it, but I'm not actually taking in what I'm supposed to do next. The information just completely stops processing, no matter how hard I'm trying to force myself to read the numbers or look at the labels. So it's definitely not that I'm not trying hard enough. I'm putting in so much mental effort just trying to hold my concentration together, but it just slips right through my fingers no matter what I do.
Do you think your difficulties with completing tasks at work would improve if you were in a less stressful job?

Less stressful... wow, um. I really don't know. I honestly haven't even thought about that, just because... well, what even counts as a less stressful job, you know? Like, I look at my friends from college who have those entry-level office jobs I was talking about, and they're always stressed about answering emails on time and sitting in endless meetings and dealing with their managers, which sounds like a totally different kind of stress. But if you mean less physically intense, or less... chaotic than a meat processing plant? I mean, maybe? But then again, I really don't know if the stress is actually what's causing the problem. 

Because, like I was just saying, when I have to do those certification modules, I'm just sitting in the breakroom. It's quiet in there, it's warm, I'm sitting in a normal chair, nobody is yelling over the machinery, there's no conveyor belt of raw poultry rushing past me... it's probably the least stressful, safest part of the entire building. And I still completely shut down. I still can't force my brain to process the words on the page or the screen. So if I was at a desk job somewhere else, a quiet, low-stress desk job, would I just be doing the exact same thing? Would I just be staring blankly at a spreadsheet instead of a sanitation log? 

I mean, college was stressful, getting my bachelor's was a ton of pressure with finals and papers, and I definitely had moments where I struggled to keep my head in the game then, too. But it just feels so much more extreme now. So maybe the environment at the plant is making it worse, with the freezing temperatures and the smell and the constant noise just draining my battery faster... but I honestly couldn't tell you for sure if an easier job would actually fix the fact that my brain just stops working. I think I'm just so caught up in trying to get through my shifts right now, literally just surviving day to day and trying not to get in trouble with Dave, that I haven't really had the mental space to imagine if I'd be better off somewhere else. So, yeah, I really don't know. I wish I did, but I just don't know.
Do you think you would have the same difficulties with completing tasks if you were to switch to a different role within the same company?

Switching to a different role... gosh, I mean, I really don't know. I haven't actually explored that, mainly because I don't even know what I would switch to, you know? Like, if I really think about the other departments in the plant... well, there's Quality Assurance, which I guess some people consider a step up from the line, but those guys are basically doing nothing but logs and clipboard work all day long. They walk around with these digital tablets taking the core temperatures of the meat vats and checking the pH levels and swabbing the stainless steel surfaces for bacteria. Which, honestly, sounds like my absolute worst nightmare, because if I'm already zoning out on my own basic sanitation logs, imagine if my entire job was just staring at numbers and tiny little checkboxes for eight hours straight. I'd probably accidentally approve a contaminated batch or something just because my brain completely glossed over a decimal point and I didn't even realize I was looking at it. 

And then there's the warehouse side, the logistics guys who drive the forklifts and load the pallets onto the refrigerated trucks out on the loading dock. But that’s still freezing cold, and it's still incredibly loud with all the backup beepers and the truck engines, and they have to be so meticulously careful with the shipping manifests and scanning the exact right barcodes for inventory. If my brain just shuts off while I'm doing that, I could literally drop a ton of frozen poultry on someone or send an entire shipment to the wrong state. 

I guess there's the front office? Like HR or accounting or something. Since I do have my bachelor's degree, maybe I could try to pivot to the corporate side of the building. But they just sit in these little grey cubicles all day under those awful buzzing fluorescent lights, staring at spreadsheets and dealing with payroll or vendor invoices. And like I was just saying about those certification modules, sitting still at a computer screen just completely drains the life out of me. It makes my brain feel like it's wrapped in heavy cotton. 

So, honestly, I really don't know. I don't know if moving to a different role would actually fix anything or if I'd just be dragging this exact same problem into a different room of the building. It really feels like no matter what the specific tasks are, my brain is just going to find a way to hit a wall with them eventually. So, yeah, I really couldn't say for sure if it would help at all.
Do you think your brain shutting off at work is directly caused by the stress of the job?

Directly caused by it? Gosh, um... I really, really don't know if I can say it's a direct cause-and-effect thing. Because, honestly, if it was just the stress causing it, wouldn't I only shut down when things are actually going wrong? Or when we're behind on a quota and Dave is pacing up and down the line yelling over the machinery? But it happens even when things are going perfectly fine. 

And I think a lot about what stress actually feels like, you know? Like, when I think of being stressed, I think of my heart racing, or my stomach in knots, or feeling really overwhelmed and panicked, like how I felt during finals week when I was finishing up my bachelor's. But when my brain shuts off at the plant, it doesn't feel like that at all. It’s actually the complete opposite. It’s not a panic, it’s just... nothing. It’s like pure static. I’ll just be standing there in the 38-degree cutting room, holding my boning knife or my clipboard, and there is zero emotion. There's no anxiety in that specific moment, just a complete and total power outage in my head. 

So it's really hard for me to confidently sit here and say, "Yes, the stress is doing this," because the shut-downs happen when I'm just wiping down a stainless steel prep table, which has absolutely zero stakes, just as much as they happen when I'm logging the core temperatures of a massive batch where a mistake could cost the company thousands of dollars. It doesn't seem to discriminate based on how high the pressure is. 

I mean, maybe the physical stress of the environment is a totally different thing? Like, maybe the sheer sensory overload of the place—the smell of the heavy-duty industrial sanitizer mixed with the raw poultry, the freezing cold that seeps into your boots no matter how many pairs of thermal socks you wear, the constant, deafening hum of the ventilation fans and the conveyor belts—maybe all of that is just constantly draining my mental battery in the background without me even realizing it. Like having too many apps open on your phone until it just dies. But as far as the actual mental stress of the job directly triggering my brain to just go blank and stop processing information? I really don't know. I wish I had a clearer answer for you, but I just can't figure out the pattern.
Do you have trouble following recipes or instructions for hobbies that involve step-by-step procedures?

Recipes and hobbies... wow. Yeah. I mean, if I try to cook something that isn't just, you know, throwing pasta in boiling water, it's usually a disaster. Like, if I try to bake, I will inevitably follow the first three steps perfectly, and then somehow completely skip over adding the baking powder, or I'll get the whole batter mixed and realize I never actually turned the oven on to preheat it. It's like my brain just cannot hold onto a sequence of instructions all the way to the finish line. 

And, honestly, that exact thing—that inability to just follow a sequence of steps all the way through—is really the main thing that brings me in to see you. Because it's not just ruining a batch of muffins at home, it's happening at work, where the stakes are so much higher. 

At the plant, everything we do is a step-by-step procedure. And the problem is that I keep starting the sanitation steps, or the batch logs, or the end-of-line paperwork, and I somehow just leave out the last parts. Like, with the sanitation steps, there's a whole process. You have to do the dry pick-up of the meat scraps, then the initial hot water rinse, then apply the foaming degreaser, then scrub, then rinse again, and then apply the final chemical sanitizer. And I'll start out doing it perfectly! I'll be scrubbing the stainless steel belts, totally focused. But then... I don't know, I just trail off. I'll completely skip the final sanitizing spray and just start putting the hoses away. 

Or with the end-of-line paperwork, there are maybe six specific boxes you have to fill out in order—the lot number, the processing time, the core temperature, the visual inspection check, and your signature. I will meticulously fill out the first four boxes, and then my brain just checks out. I'll literally just put the clipboard down and walk away, leaving the last two sections completely blank. 

And the worst part is, I *know* my job depends on finishing them correctly. Dave, my floor manager, has drilled it into our heads that the USDA inspectors can shut down the line or fine the company massive amounts of money if those logs aren't filled out to the very last checkbox. The stakes are incredibly high. I am fully aware of how important it is, and I desperately need this job to pay off the student loans from my bachelor's. But even knowing all of that, even knowing I could get fired, I still just drop the ball right at the end of the instructions. It's like my brain reaches a certain point in a multi-step process and just decides, "Okay, we're done here," even when there are clearly crucial steps left. It's so frustrating because I'm trying so hard, but I just can't seem to make myself finish the whole sequence.
Do you have trouble remembering instructions or tasks that you need to complete later in the day?

Later in the day... hmm. Let me really think about how that plays out on the floor. You mean like if someone gives me an instruction in the morning and I have to remember to do it hours later? 

Honestly, I don't think I really have a problem with that. Which is kind of weird, right? Like, you'd think my brain would just drop that information entirely, considering how bad I am at finishing a basic sequence of steps in the moment. But it doesn't really happen like that. 

For example, we have these pre-shift huddles at 6:00 AM every morning. We all stand around in the breakroom—which, by the way, always smells faintly of industrial bleach and stale coffee, it's a terrible combination—and Dave will go over the daily quotas or tell us if there's a specific piece of machinery that needs extra attention during the mid-shift breakdown. And if he points at me and says, "Hey, make sure you double-check the calibration on the vacuum sealer after the 1:30 lunch rotation," I actually *will* remember at 1:30 that I'm supposed to go do it. The instruction itself somehow stays locked in my head. I'll watch the clock, and I'll walk right over to the vacuum sealer right on time. 

It's just that once I'm actually standing there, trying to do the steps to calibrate it, *that's* when the short-circuit happens and I end up leaving the last half of the log blank or I forget to turn the safety latch back on. But the actual remembering to initiate the task later in the day? No, I don't really think I struggle with that. I mean, at least not that I've noticed. 

It's the same thing outside of work, too. Like if my mom calls me on my morning break and says, "Don't forget to stop at the pharmacy on your way home to pick up your prescription," I'll remember to drive to the pharmacy at 4:00 PM. The instruction sticks. Now, I might walk into the pharmacy and get completely derailed by the greeting card aisle or just feel totally drained and zone out at the register, but the actual memory that I needed to go there later in the day is intact. So, yeah, I wouldn't say remembering future instructions is really the issue for me. It's more about the immediate follow-through once I'm actually doing the thing, if that makes sense?
Do you think your difficulties with completing tasks would still exist if you were doing the same type of work in a quieter, less stressful environment?

Gosh, a quieter, less stressful environment doing this same type of work? I honestly... I really don't know. I mean, I don't even know if a quiet meat processing environment actually exists anywhere in the real world, you know? Like, maybe if I worked at some tiny, boutique, artisanal butcher shop in a small town where they only process one locally sourced pig a week and play classical music in the background? But even then, you'd still have the bone saws and the industrial grinders, so it's hard to even picture what a quiet version of my job would look like. 

Because I've never experienced it, I don't really have a baseline to compare it to. I want to say that, yeah, maybe taking away all that intense sensory overload—the deafening ventilation fans, the freezing cold that just aches in your toes, Dave constantly yelling over the conveyor belts—maybe taking all of that away would magically fix my ability to just finish a task. Because like I said, it does feel like that environment is constantly draining my mental battery. 

But then again... if I really sit here and think about it, I don't know if the noise and stress are actually the root of the problem. Because I think about what I told you earlier, about baking at home. My apartment kitchen is perfectly quiet. There's no pressure, no USDA inspectors, no one yelling at me, and it's definitely not thirty-eight degrees. It's as low-stress as you can possibly get. And yet, I still completely drop the ball on the sequence of steps. I still leave out the baking powder or forget to turn the oven on. 

So if you took me out of the plant and put me in a perfectly silent, room-temperature room, and handed me that exact same clipboard with the six boxes for the end-of-line paperwork... would I actually fill out the last two boxes? Or would my brain still just hit that invisible wall and check out? I genuinely don't know. Part of me thinks that in a completely silent room, my brain would just find the silence itself distracting, like how when it's too quiet you just start hearing the blood pumping in your own ears, you know? Or maybe I'd just zone out staring at the blank wall instead of zoning out staring at the stainless steel prep table. 

It's just so hard to untangle what's the environment and what's just... me. Especially since I've only ever done this specific work in this one extremely loud, high-pressure plant right after finishing my bachelor's. I wish I could give you a straightforward yes or no, but without ever having tried it, I just really couldn't say for sure either way.
Do you think you would experience the same difficulties with completing tasks if you were doing a completely different type of work?

A completely different type of work... wow, I mean... I honestly have no idea. I really don't. Because, you know, I just finished my bachelor's degree not that long ago, and this job at the processing plant is really the only full-time, real-world job I’ve ever had. I took it because, like I said, the student loans are just crushing, and the plant pays a decent hourly rate with all the mandatory overtime, even if it means I’m coming home smelling like raw poultry and industrial sanitizer every single day. So I don't really have anything to compare it to, you know? 

Like, if I were doing something completely different... say, if I actually used my degree and got some sort of office job. Like, sitting in a cubicle, answering emails, maybe doing marketing or data entry or something where you wear actual clothes instead of a giant rubber apron, a hairnet, and steel-toed boots. I sit there on the line sometimes and just daydream about what that would be like, just sitting in a rolling chair with a cup of coffee that isn't from a breakroom vending machine. But if I was doing *that* kind of work... would I still have this problem? I honestly couldn't tell you. 

Because on one hand, maybe I wouldn't be so physically exhausted, and maybe my brain wouldn't be so overwhelmed by the sheer physical demand of the plant. But on the other hand... a sequence is a sequence, right?
